content: Diarrhea is an infrequent gastrointestinal symptom in patients with COVID-19, but it can occasionally be the initial presenting symptom in some cases. The reported frequency of diarrhea in COVID-19 patients ranges from 1% to 35%, with significant variability across studies, likely due to differing definitions of diarrhea used in research. A higher prevalence of diarrhea has been observed in patients with severe COVID-19 compared to those with milder forms of the disease. Additionally, patients presenting with gastrointestinal symptoms, including diarrhea, are more likely to develop severe respiratory complications, such as acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), which may necessitate ventilatory support. Pathophysiology SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for COVID-19, gains entry into human cells by binding to angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) receptors and utilizing the serine protease TMPRSS2. These receptors are not only abundant in the lungs but are also highly expressed in the enterocytes of the small intestine. Other sites of ACE2 receptor expression in the gastrointestinal tract include the upper esophagus, liver, and colon. Once the virus enters the gastrointestinal tract, it can disrupt the integrity of enterocytes, leading to inflammation and alterations in intestinal permeability. This disruption may contribute to the development of diarrhea. Furthermore, the use of various antiviral and antibiotic treatments for COVID-19 may alter the gut microbiota, potentially exacerbating diarrhea. Clinical Features of Diarrhea Caused by SARS-CoV-2 According to Jin et al., diarrhea in COVID-19 patients is defined as the passage of loose stools more than three times per day. Approximately 1% of patients experience diarrhea at the onset of illness, with symptoms lasting an average of four days. Other studies have reported that the duration of diarrhea ranges from two to four days, with patients experiencing three to eight bowel movements per day. Treatment The primary approach to managing diarrhea in COVID-19 patients is supportive care. Key components of treatment include rehydration, fluid replacement, and monitoring of potassium levels to prevent electrolyte imbalances. The use of probiotics may be beneficial, particularly if diarrhea is linked to disruptions in the gut microbiome. Probiotics could also play a role in preventing secondary bacterial infections by restoring the balance of gut microbiota.
